title: Bathtub parameters
$comment: Slider granularity is x-step, NOT multipleOf. multipleOf is checked by floating-point division, and 1.4 / 0.1 is 13.999999999999998 - so a schema declaring multipleOf 0.1 rejects 16 of the 51 positions its own slider can reach, this sandbox's own _example submission among them. x-step draws the control; minimum and maximum do the validating. Property ORDER is the panel order and is deliberate: pick a future, get a water height, add what sits on top of it, then choose how the model tests it, then how it is drawn. x-group starts a new labelled section; x-disabled-when greys a control out while another control is making its decision for it, and its value may be a LIST, meaning any one of these takes the control over.

year.title: How far ahead
year.description: The five dates the panel reports. Notice the spread grows faster than the water does: in the 2030s the four projections are within 18cm of each other, and by 2150 they run from 1.0m to 4.5m. Past about 2080, which projection you pick matters more than which year.

percentile.title: Which projection
percentile.description: Sea level rise is published as a range, not a number. The New York City Panel on Climate Change gives four of them for each date and deliberately does not give a middle value. So there is no "the" projection to draw. Every flood map you have seen picked one of these four on your behalf, and most of them didn't say which.

link_year.title: Take sea level from the projection
link_year.description: On, the water height comes from the date and projection you chose above, and the slider below is set for you. Off, you set it by hand. Setting it by hand is the honest way to poke at the model and find out what the terrain does. It is also how you make a map that means nothing, because no date is attached to it.

slr_m.title: Sea level rise
slr_m.description: How much higher the average sea sits than it does now. Everything below adds onto this one number, and there is no map of it - the model raises the whole harbour by the same amount at once.

aep.title: Storm, by how often
aep.description: Pick a storm by how often it happens rather than by how high it is. These are NOAA's exceedance probability levels for the gauge at the Battery: the 1% level is the one with a 1-in-100 chance of being reached in any given year, and it is 2.51m above NAVD88, read for October 2025 - the levels ride the sea level trend, so they carry a date. Two things about them are worth knowing before you trust the map. They are fitted to the highest water level of each year, and the highest water level of a year happens at high tide - so the tide is already inside the number, which is why choosing one here takes the tide control over instead of adding to it. And they are still-water levels: no waves. The 1% is about 8.2 feet; Sandy reached about 11.3 feet at this same gauge. If you pick "100-year" and see less water than you remember, you are looking at two definitions, not at a bug.

surge_m.title: Storm surge, by hand
surge_m.description: The override. Set a height yourself and read off, from the control above, roughly how often the water gets that high. Whichever way you set it, it just gets added to the water height, instantly and everywhere at once. A real surge arrives over hours, peaks, drains, and is higher in some places than others.

tide.title: Tide state
tide.description: The sea is not at one height. At the Battery it swings about a metre and a half between low and high. Pick which moment of that swing the map is showing. Published flood maps usually use the average daily high tide, which is the cautious choice - it's the default here. These three numbers come from one gauge at the tip of Manhattan and are applied to the whole city; NOAA uses a tidal surface that varies from place to place. Pick a storm probability and this control goes quiet, because an exceedance level already contains a high tide: NOAA states the 1% level as 1.82m above the average daily high tide, and that is the same 2.51m written the other way round.

connectivity.title: Hydraulic connectivity
connectivity.description: Water has to get somewhere from somewhere. On: a place floods only if there is an unbroken path of low ground between it and open water. Off: everything below the waterline floods, including inland dips the sea can't reach. The red patches on the map are the difference between the two. Almost every published flood map does apply connectivity, and is still a bathtub model.

basemap.title: Shade by water depth
basemap.description: Shaded colours the flood darker where the water is deeper, up to six metres. It is the same threshold either way - this only changes how it's drawn. Flat is closer to how most published flood maps look, which is worth comparing.

flood_line.title: Flood line
flood_line.description: The dark edge between wet and dry. It isn't a dataset we downloaded. It's found by looking for wet cells that sit next to dry ones, which is how every flood boundary you have seen was made. Zoom right in and you can watch it turn into a staircase of grid cells.
